title: Alphabet and pronunciation
summary: Norwegian has 29 letters and a fairly regular spelling, but a few sounds (æ, ø, å, kj, sj) and silent letters trip up English speakers.

blocks.text: The alphabet is the English one plus **æ, ø, å** at the end (a-z, æ, ø, å). C, q, w, x and z only appear in loanwords. Stress usually falls on the first syllable, and Norwegian has two word tones (pitch accents) that distinguish a few word pairs.

blocks.caption: Tricky letters and letter combinations
head: Spelling
Sound (approximate)
Example
rows: like a in 'cat' (short) or a stretched 'bad' (long)
like 'u' in British 'fur'; say 'e' with rounded lips
like German ü or French u; say 'ee' with rounded lips
a rounded vowel between English 'oo' and y
like 'h' in 'huge' (a soft ch as in German ich)
like English 'y' in 'yes' (the first letter is silent)
g before i, y, ei, øy
d after a vowel or l/n at word end, t in 'det'

items: **Tone**: accent 1 (a simple fall) vs accent 2 (a fall-rise) separates words like bønder (farmers, accent 1) and bønner (beans or prayers, accent 2). You can be understood without it; learn it gradually by listening.
**Double consonants** mean the vowel before is short: tak (roof) vs takk (thanks); hel vs hell.
**Pronunciation varies** a lot by dialect (the r can be rolled or uvular); follow the Oslo (East Norwegian) standard when in doubt.

items.no: Jeg kjøper en kjole i Kjeller.
items.en: I am buying a dress in Kjeller.

items.no: Hva sa hun om sjokoladen?
items.en: What did she say about the chocolate? (practice: hv-, sj)

items.no: Gjør du hjemmeleksene dine?
items.en: Are you doing your homework?

items.no: Det er en pen jente på bildet.
items.en: There is a pretty girl in the picture.

blocks.text: Don't read **å** as English 'a' or **ø** as 'o'. Mixing up the three extra vowels is the most common spelling mistake: bær (berry), bør (should), bor (lives) and bar are all different words.

title: Nouns: gender and plural
summary: Every noun is masculine (en), feminine (ei) or neuter (et), and the gender decides articles, adjective endings and the plural.

blocks.text: Bokmål has three genders, but feminine nouns can also be treated as masculine, so many speakers only use **en** and **et**. Learn each noun with its article: en bil, ei jente, et hus. Neuter nouns are the group that behaves differently in the plural.

blocks.caption: Gender with indefinite, definite and plural forms
head: Indefinite
Definite
Plural
Definite plural
Pattern

items: **en**: nouns in -ing, -else, -dom, -sjon and agents in -er (en lærer).
**et**: nouns in -skap, -ment, -(i)um (et vennskap, et dokument, et museum) and most nouns for small or abstract things.
**ei/en**: nouns in -het (ei/en frihet); a few common ones are almost always feminine: ei bok, ei jente, ei klokke.
Foreign nouns often take -er: en student, studenter; en bank, banker. Some are the same in plural: et tema, temaer.

items.no: Jeg har to søsken og tre katter.
items.en: I have two siblings and three cats.

items.no: Barna leker i hagen.
items.en: The children are playing in the garden.

items.no: Vi kjøpte fem bøker og et eple.
items.en: We bought five books and an apple.

items.no: Hendene mine er kalde.
items.en: My hands are cold.

blocks.text: Neuter plurals look the same as the singular: et hus, to **hus** (not to huser). When learning, always memorise en/ei/et together with the noun.

title: Articles and double definiteness
summary: The definite article is a suffix on the noun (bilen, huset), and it is repeated with adjectives and demonstratives.

blocks.text: The indefinite article (a/an) is a separate word before the noun: **en, ei, et**. The definite article (the) is attached to the end of the noun. When an adjective or demonstrative comes before the noun, you also add a separate word (den/det/de), which is called **double definiteness**.

blocks.caption: Indefinite, definite and double definite forms
head: Gender
Indefinite
Definite
With adjective (definite)
Plural definite with adjective

items: Nouns ending in -e only add -n (en) or -t (et): gutten, eplet; feminine nouns often take -a (jenta, boka).
**Demonstratives**: denne/dette/disse (this, these); den/det/de (that, those, with stress); the noun is always in the definite form after them.
**No article** for professions and nationalities (Jeg er lærer), for languages (Jeg snakker norsk), and for general mass nouns (Jeg liker kaffe).
**Possessives**: either before the noun with an indefinite noun (min bil) or after the noun with a definite noun (bilen min). The second is more common.

items.no: Den røde bilen er min.
items.en: The red car is mine.

items.no: Jeg liker det gamle huset.
items.en: I like the old house.

items.no: Er du student eller lærer?
items.en: Are you a student or a teacher?

items.no: Denne boka er veldig god.
items.en: This book is very good.

blocks.text: Don't say 'store bilen'. With an adjective you need **den** + adjective + noun-with-suffix: **den store bilen**. Exceptions: with a possessive you only use the adjective: min store bil / den store bilen min.

title: Pronouns: personal, possessive and reflexive
summary: Norwegian pronouns change by case and possessives agree with the noun; reflexive sin/si/sitt/sine refers back to the subject.

blocks.caption: Possessives (placed after a definite noun: bilen min)
head: Owner
en-noun
ei-noun
et-noun
plural

blocks.text: Use **sin/si/sitt/sine** only when the owner is the **subject of the same clause** and is third person. Use **hans/hennes/deres** when the owner is someone else. Only the reflexive agrees with the thing owned; hans, hennes and deres never change.

items.no: Hun ser på seg selv i speilet.
items.en: She looks at herself in the mirror.

items.no: Jeg ringte ham, men han svarte ikke.
items.en: I called him, but he didn't answer.

items.no: Vi gleder oss til ferien vår.
items.en: We are looking forward to our holiday.

items.no: Per og kona hans bor i Bergen.
items.en: Per and his wife live in Bergen.

blocks.text: Sin/si/sitt/sine is never used for the subject itself and never for 1st/2nd person (you say min, din). 'Han og hans bror' is fine, but 'Han elsker hans bil' is wrong if the car is his own: say **sin bil**.

title: Adjectives: agreement and comparison
summary: Adjectives change form for neuter and plural/definite nouns, and form comparatives and superlatives with -ere/-est or mer/mest.

blocks.text: In a predicate the adjective agrees with the subject: Bilen er stor, Huset er stort, Husene er store. Before a noun it agrees with the noun and, with definite nouns, takes **-e** in all cases: den store bilen, det store huset.

items: Comparison with **enn**: Hun er eldre enn meg. Equality with **like ... som**: Han er like høy som henne.
Superlatives take the definite form when used before a noun: den største byen, det beste huset.
The comparative never changes for gender or number: en større bil, et større hus, større biler.

items.no: Det er et stort og gammelt hus.
items.en: It is a big, old house.

items.no: Dette er den beste kaffen i byen.
items.en: This is the best coffee in town.

items.no: Bergen er mindre enn Oslo, men vakrere.
items.en: Bergen is smaller than Oslo, but more beautiful.

items.no: Jeg har flere venner enn før.
items.en: I have more friends than before.

blocks.text: Remember **flere** (more of something countable), **mer** (more of something uncountable) and **mange** vs **mye**: mange venner, mye penger. 'Mer' also forms comparatives of longer adjectives.

title: Verbs: present, past, perfect and infinitive
summary: Norwegian verbs do not change with the subject; you only need the infinitive, present, past and perfect participle forms.

blocks.text: The infinitive ends in a vowel (usually -e) and is preceded by **å**: å spise. The present adds **-r** (spiser), the past has an ending (-et, -te, -de, -dde) or a vowel change for strong verbs, and the perfect is **har** + the perfect participle (supine). The imperative is the bare stem: Spis! Kom!

items: Use the **past (preteritum)** for a finished time: Jeg var i Oslo i fjor.
Use the **perfect** for experience or relevance now: Jeg har vært i Oslo (at some point), Jeg har bodd her i to år (and still do).
Norwegian always uses **har** with the perfect, even for movement verbs: Jeg har gått hjem, not 'er gått'.
Future: Jeg skal reise i morgen (plan), Det kommer til å regne (prediction). Present tense also works for the future: Vi reiser i morgen.
No continuous tense: Jeg spiser = I eat / I am eating. Use **sitter og leser**, **holder på å** for ongoing actions.

items.no: Jeg bor i Oslo, men jeg vokste opp i Bergen.
items.en: I live in Oslo, but I grew up in Bergen.

items.no: Har du spist middag ennå?
items.en: Have you eaten dinner yet?

items.no: I går kjøpte vi en ny bil.
items.en: Yesterday we bought a new car.

items.no: Hun har skrevet tre bøker.
items.en: She has written three books.

items.no: Vi holder på å lage mat.
items.en: We are in the middle of cooking.

blocks.text: The verb never changes with the subject: jeg er, du er, de er. Don't confuse **bli** (become, stay: Jeg blir hjemme) with **være** (be).

title: Modal verbs
summary: Modals (kan, må, vil, skal, bør, får, tør) are followed by a bare infinitive without å and have a special present form.

blocks.text: Modal verbs express ability, obligation, wish, plan or permission. The main verb that follows is in the **infinitive without å**, and the modal takes the second position in main clauses.

blocks.caption: Modal verbs
head: Infinitive
Present
Past
Perfect
Meaning
rows: can, be able to, know how to
shall, be going to, be supposed to

blocks.caption: Meanings and usage hints
head: Modal
Typical use
Example
rows: trenger ikke å / behøver ikke å
Jeg tør ikke å si det.

items: Same form in the present for all persons: jeg kan, du kan, de kan.
**Ikke** goes after the modal: Jeg kan ikke komme. Two verbs: Jeg har ikke villet gå.
Perfect with a modal: Jeg har villet gjøre det, Jeg har måttet jobbe. Motion verbs can be dropped: Jeg må hjem (må + dra).
**Kommer til å** + infinitive predicts the future: Det kommer til å regne.

items.no: Kan du hjelpe meg?
items.en: Can you help me?

items.no: Jeg må jobbe i morgen.
items.en: I have to work tomorrow.

items.no: Vi skal på kino i kveld.
items.en: We are going to the cinema tonight.

items.no: Du bør ikke spise så mye sukker.
items.en: You shouldn't eat so much sugar.

items.no: Jeg vil gjerne ha en kopp te.
items.en: I would like a cup of tea.

blocks.text: Don't use **å** after a modal: Jeg kan **å** snakke is wrong. And **må ikke** means 'must not', not 'don't have to' (that is trenger ikke).

title: Word order: the V2 rule
summary: In a main clause the finite verb is always in second position, so the subject goes after the verb when something else comes first.

blocks.text: Main clauses follow the **V2 rule**: whatever stands first (subject, time, place, object, a subordinate clause), the conjugated verb comes second. When the first element is not the subject, the subject moves behind the verb. This is called **inversion**.

blocks.caption: V2 and inversion
head: 1st position
Verb
Subject
Rest
English
rows: Because it rained, we stayed home.
I have eaten dinner (verb pair split).

items: With **two verbs** (modal, har + participle): the finite verb stays in position 2 and the other verb goes to the end: Vi har spist. I går **har** vi spist ute.
**Place before time** is the default when both appear after the verb: Jeg reiser til Oslo i morgen.
**Coordinating conjunctions** (og, men, eller, for, så) don't affect the order: Jeg er trøtt, så jeg går hjem. (As an adverb 'så' = then triggers inversion: Så gikk jeg hjem.)
**Yes/no questions** and **imperatives** start with the verb: Snakker du norsk? Kom hit!
Direct and indirect objects: Jeg ga henne boka. (pronoun objects can come before ikke: Jeg så ham ikke.)

items.no: I dag har jeg vært på jobb.
items.en: Today I have been at work.

items.no: Etter filmen gikk vi hjem.
items.en: After the film we went home.

items.no: Hjemme snakker vi norsk.
items.en: At home we speak Norwegian.

items.no: Plutselig kom det en bil.
items.en: Suddenly a car came.

blocks.text: A very common error for English speakers: 'I morgen jeg reiser'. After any fronted element, the verb comes before the subject: **I morgen reiser jeg**.

title: Negation and adverb placement
summary: Ikke and sentence adverbs come after the verb in main clauses but before the verb in subordinate clauses.

blocks.text: The Norwegian word for 'not' is **ikke** ('inte' is Swedish). Sentence adverbs such as aldri, alltid, ofte, også, bare, nok, jo, vel and sikkert follow the same placement rule as ikke.

blocks.caption: Where ikke and adverbs go
head: Clause type
Position
Example
rows: after the finite verb/subject, before the second verb
Jeg vet at han ikke kommer.
Jeg tror at hun alltid drikker te.

blocks.caption: Other negatives
head: Word
Meaning
Example
rows: Jeg har aldri vært i Tromsø.
Verken du eller jeg vet svaret.

items.no: Jeg snakker ikke fransk.
items.en: I don't speak French.

items.no: Han sa at han ikke hadde tid.
items.en: He said that he had no time.

items.no: Hvis du ikke kommer, blir jeg skuffet.
items.en: If you don't come, I will be disappointed.

items.no: Du kan ikke bare gå.
items.en: You can't just leave.

blocks.text: Use **ikke**, not 'inte'. And no do-support: 'Jeg liker ikke' (not 'jeg gjør ikke like'). In a subordinate clause the adverb jumps in front of the verb: ... fordi jeg **ikke** har tid.

title: Questions and question words
summary: Yes/no questions start with the verb; wh-questions start with a question word followed by the verb and then the subject.

blocks.caption: Question words
head: Question word
Meaning
Example
rows: Hvor lenge har du bodd her?

items: **Yes/no**: verb + subject: Snakker du norsk? Har du tid? Kan du hjelpe meg?
**Wh-question**: question word + verb + subject: Hva gjør du? When the question word is the subject, there is no extra subject: Hvem bor her?
**Prepositions** go at the end in spoken Norwegian: Hva venter du på? Hvem snakker du med?
**Answering negatives**: use **jo** for 'yes' to a negative question: Snakker du ikke norsk? — Jo, det gjør jeg. Use **nei** to confirm the negative.
**Tags**: add ikke sant? Du kommer i morgen, ikke sant?
**Indirect questions** use subordinate order: Jeg lurer på hvor han bor. Jeg vet ikke hva hun ikke liker.

items.no: Hva gjør du i helgen?
items.en: What are you doing this weekend?

items.no: Hvorfor kom du ikke i går?
items.en: Why didn't you come yesterday?

items.no: Hvilket hus bor du i?
items.en: Which house do you live in?

items.no: Vet du hvor stasjonen er?
items.en: Do you know where the station is?

blocks.text: No 'do' in questions. Say **Snakker du norsk?**, not 'Gjør du snakke norsk?'. And **hva** is 'what', while **hvilken** means 'which' and agrees with the noun.

title: Subordinate clauses and conjunctions
summary: Subordinators such as at, som, fordi, hvis, når and selv om introduce a clause in which adverbs go before the verb.

blocks.caption: Common subordinating conjunctions
head: Conjunction
Meaning
Example
rows: Mannen som bor her, er lærer.
Jeg er hjemme fordi jeg er syk.
Siden det regner, blir vi inne.
Hvis du vil, kan du komme.
Jeg lurer på om han kommer.
Når jeg kommer hjem, spiser jeg.
Da jeg var liten, bodde vi i Bergen.
Jeg leste mens hun lagde mat.
Etter at vi spiste, gikk vi tur.
Jeg går ut selv om det regner.
Jeg snakker saktere slik at du forstår.
Hun er eldre enn han er.

items: **Word order** inside the clause: conjunction + subject + adverb/ikke + verb: ... fordi jeg ikke har tid.
If the subordinate clause comes **first**, the main clause is inverted (V2): Fordi jeg er syk, er jeg hjemme.
**at** can be dropped after tro, tenke, synes, si, mene; if so, use main-clause order: Jeg tror han ikke kommer.
**som** is needed as a subject relative ('Jeg ser mannen som bor her'); it is often dropped as an object: Boka (som) jeg leste, var god.
**Hvis** for conditions, **om** for indirect yes/no questions: Hvis det regner ... / Jeg vet ikke om det regner.

items.no: Jeg vet ikke om hun kommer, fordi hun ikke har svart.
items.en: I don't know whether she is coming, because she hasn't answered.

items.no: Selv om jeg er trøtt, må jeg jobbe.
items.en: Even though I am tired, I have to work.

items.no: Når han kommer, spiser vi.
items.en: When he comes, we will eat.

items.no: Jeg liker bøker som er korte.
items.en: I like books that are short.

blocks.text: Don't mix up **når** (future or habit) and **da** (single past event): 'Da jeg kom hjem, var det mørkt.' 'Når jeg kommer hjem, ringer jeg.' Also avoid inverting inside the clause: 'at han kommer ikke' is wrong; say **at han ikke kommer**.

title: Prepositions of place and time
summary: Choosing between på, i, til, fra, med, av and om is mostly idiomatic, so learn them with set phrases.

blocks.caption: Core prepositions
head: Preposition
Place use
Time or other use
Example
rows: inside, in a country or city, a closed space
months, years, durations: i juni, i år, i to timer
Jeg bor i Oslo. Vi har ventet i en time.
on a surface; open places, islands, events, public transport
weekdays: på mandag; languages: på norsk
Boka ligger på bordet. Jeg er på jobb. Vi tok bussen på mandag.
Jeg reiser til Bergen. Vi venter til fredag.
Hun er fra Norge. Jeg jobber fra åtte til fire.
Jeg reiser med tog. Jeg bor med kjæresten min.
Boka er skrevet av henne. Bordet er laget av tre.
in (future), in the morning/evening/summer: om morgenen, om to uker
Vi snakket om været. Jeg kommer om en time.
Det er for deg. Jeg flyttet hit for to år siden.
Banken ligger mellom skolen og kafeen.
in front of / behind / next to

items: **i** a country or city, **på** an island or at an institution/event: i Norge, på Island, på skolen, på kino, på jobb, på fest.
Public transport uses **på** (på bussen, på toget), and cars and taxis use **i**.
**Verb + preposition** combos to learn: vente på, tenke på, glede seg til, være redd for, snakke om, være gift med, være interessert i.

items.no: Jeg bor i Oslo, men jobber på sykehuset.
items.en: I live in Oslo, but I work at the hospital.

items.no: Vi drar til Spania i juli.
items.en: We are going to Spain in July.

items.no: Hun kommer fra Tyskland og snakker på norsk med meg.
items.en: She comes from Germany and speaks Norwegian with me.

items.no: Jeg ser deg om to dager.
items.en: I will see you in two days.

blocks.text: Norwegian distinguishes location and direction: **Jeg er hjemme / Jeg går hjem**; **Han er ute / Han går ut**. Don't say 'Jeg går til hjem'.

title: Passive voice
summary: Norwegian forms the passive with an -s ending on the verb or with bli + the perfect participle.

blocks.text: The passive moves the focus from the doer to the thing affected. Both forms are common. The **-s passive** is short and used for general statements, rules and the present tense. The **bli-passive** is used for specific events and often names the doer with **av**.

blocks.caption: The two passives
head: Active
-s passive
bli passive
rows: Boka har blitt skrevet av ham.

blocks.caption: How to form each
head: Tense
-s passive
bli passive
rows: har blitt + participle: har blitt åpnet
å bli åpnet, kan bli bygget

items: Use **bli** when there is an agent or a one-time event: Huset ble solgt av naboen.
Use **-s** for rules, signs, instructions and generalisations: Her røykes det ikke. Brødet selges her.
Some verbs always end in -s (deponent): synes, trives, finnes, møtes, minnes. These are not passive: Jeg synes det er bra.
**Det** is often a dummy subject: Det spilles musikk.

items.no: Huset ble bygget i 1950.
items.en: The house was built in 1950.

items.no: Norsk snakkes av fem millioner mennesker.
items.en: Norwegian is spoken by five million people.

items.no: Brevet blir sendt i dag.
items.en: The letter will be sent today.

items.no: Vi trives godt her.
items.en: We like it here (deponent verb, not passive).

blocks.text: Don't use 'være' for the passive of events: 'Huset var bygget' describes a state (it was built/existed), while **Huset ble bygget** describes the action of building.

title: Numbers, dates and clock time
summary: Learn the cardinals, ordinals, how to say dates and years, and the unusual 'halv' system for telling the time.

blocks.text: Compound numbers are written as one word with the unit first: 21 = tjueen,34 = trettifire, 99 = nittini, 125 = hundre og tjuefem. The year 1984 is nitten åttifire; 2024 is tjuetjuefire or totusen og tjuefire. Use **en/ei/ett** depending on gender: en bil, ei jente, ett hus (the numeral ett is stressed).

items: **Dates**: write 17. mai, say syttende mai: Det er den første januar. Months and weekdays are written with a small letter: januar, mandag.
**Weekdays**: mandag, tirsdag, onsdag, torsdag, fredag, lørdag, søndag. **Months**: januar, februar, mars, april, mai, juni, juli, august, september, oktober, november, desember.
**Asking the time**: Hva er klokka? Hvor mye er klokka? Answer: Klokka er tre. At a time: Møtet er klokka tre / kl. 15.
**Halv** is **half to** the next hour: halv fire = 3:30 (not 4:30).

blocks.caption: Telling the time
head: Time
Norwegian
Alternative / note
rows: tjue over tre is also used

items.no: Klokka er halv åtte.
items.en: It is half past seven.

items.no: Vi møtes klokka kvart over ti.
items.en: We meet at a quarter past ten.

items.no: Jeg ble født den tolvte mars nitten nittifem.
items.en: I was born on 12 March 1995.

items.no: Toget går klokka fjorten tretti.
items.en: The train leaves at 14:30.

blocks.text: 'Halv fire' means 3:30, not 4:30. Think 'half **way to** four'. In written or official contexts (timetables) use the 24-hour clock: 15.30.

title: Common expressions and politeness
summary: Norwegians use du with everyone, so politeness comes from set phrases such as takk, vær så snill and unnskyld.

blocks.text: Norwegian is informal: the formal pronoun De is obsolete, and you use **du** with everyone, including your boss and strangers. Politeness is expressed through words such as **takk**, **vær så snill** and **unnskyld**, and through softeners like **gjerne** and **kunne**.

blocks.caption: Greetings, thanks and apologies
head: Situation
Informal
Formal / notes
rows: Hvordan går det? / Hvordan har du det?
answer: Bra, takk. Og med deg?
Jeg forstår ikke. Kan du snakke saktere?

items: **Polite requests**: Kan jeg få en kaffe? Jeg vil gjerne ha en kaffe, takk. Kan du hjelpe meg?
**Takk** is used very often, for example after a question is answered or when paying; Norwegians say takk for all kinds of things.
**Vær så god** is said when handing something over or inviting someone to start eating; **vær så snill** is 'please' in a request.
**Wishes**: God tur! God helg! God jul! Godt nytt år! God bedring! (get well).

items.no: Unnskyld, hvor er toalettet?
items.en: Excuse me, where is the toilet?

items.no: Kan jeg få regningen, takk?
items.en: Could I have the bill, please?

items.no: Takk for hjelpen! – Bare hyggelig.
items.en: Thanks for your help! – My pleasure.

items.no: Hyggelig å treffe deg. Jeg heter Anna.
items.en: Nice to meet you. My name is Anna.

blocks.text: Don't translate 'please' as **vær så snill** in every case. It is stronger than English 'please'; use **takk** or **gjerne** instead: 'En kaffe, takk.' 'Jeg vil gjerne ha ...'.

title: Bokmål vs Nynorsk and common pitfalls
summary: Norway has two written standards, and English speakers regularly stumble on false friends and a handful of structural habits.

blocks.text: Norway has two official written standards: **Bokmål** (used by roughly 85-90% of people, and the standard in this course) and **Nynorsk** (based on rural dialects). Both are taught in school and understood by all Norwegians. Spoken Norwegian is dialectal and there is no single spoken standard.

items: **Capitalisation**: nationalities, languages, weekdays and months are lower case: norsk, mandag, juni. Jeg is lower case too.
**Posture verbs** are paired: sitte / sette (sit / put), ligge / legge (lie / lay), stå / stille (stand / place).
**Age**: Jeg er 30 år (gammel), not 'Jeg har 30 år'.
**Name**: Jeg heter Anna (not 'jeg er heter'). **Like**: Jeg liker å lese, Jeg liker kaffe.
**Perfect** takes **har**: Jeg har kommet, not 'jeg er kommet'.
**Use ikke**, not 'inte'; **hjemme/hjem**, **her/hit** show location vs direction.
**Word order**: verb second and before ikke only in main clauses; do not use 'do' in questions.

items.no: Han er gift og har to barn.
items.en: He is married and has two children.

items.no: Det var heldigvis ledig på toget.
items.en: Fortunately there was space free on the train.

items.no: Hun er veldig flink på skolen.
items.en: She is very good (diligent) at school.

items.no: Jeg har vært hjemme siden mandag.
items.en: I have been at home since Monday.

blocks.text: When you meet Nynorsk, spot the pattern: eg, ikkje, kva, ein/eit, -a for infinitives and a few vowel differences. You can read both, but write Bokmål unless a course or school says otherwise.
